title: Finding Evidence - Guided Practice
description: Learn to match evidence to the exact claim it supports, separate direct evidence from merely related details, and verify the connection across an argument.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewer: Chee Skool Finding Evidence reference-skill review
reviewNotes: Guided Finding Evidence path focused on exact claim-to-evidence matching, directness, and evidence for different reasons within one workplace argument. Existing tutoring practice remains the independent follow-up. Excluded from Mock because it contains guided support and directly taught material.

curriculum.learningObjective: Match evidence to the exact argumentative claim it supports and distinguish direct support from background, limitations, or evidence for a different claim.

questions.prompt: Match each passage detail to the claim it most directly supports.

items.text: The share of inbound trucks waiting more than fifteen minutes fell from 38 percent to 17 percent.
Late morning clock-ins fell from 11.8 percent to 6.4 percent.
Park recommends continuing the staggered schedule for six more months.
The average 7:05 entrance queue fell from twenty-six vehicles to fourteen.

explanation.answer: i1 and i4 are congestion evidence; i2 is punctuality evidence; i3 is the recommendation itself.
explanation.whyCorrect: The truck-wait and queue measures function as evidence for congestion, while clock-in records function as evidence for punctuality. Park’s recommendation is a claim about what the center should do next, not evidence for either benefit.
explanation.quickTip: Evidence can be strong and still belong to the wrong claim. Name the claim first, then ask what the detail actually measures.

questions.hint: First separate the recommendation from observed results. Then ask which exact claim each measured result can support.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives the most direct evidence for Park's claim that punctuality improved during the staggered schedule?

targets.text: During the eight weeks before the pilot, 11.8 percent of morning clock-ins were more than five minutes late.
During the staggered schedule, the rate was 6.4 percent.
A follow-up survey found that some employees on the 7:15 start said they could use a later public-bus connection instead of paying for a ride when they missed the earlier bus.
However, Park does not use the survey alone as proof of improved punctuality; the clock-in records are the direct measure of whether workers arrived on time.

explanation.answer: During the staggered schedule, the rate was 6.4 percent.
explanation.whyCorrect: This result is the direct outcome measure for the claim about improved punctuality. The survey offers a possible explanation, but the clock-in rate is what records whether late arrivals actually became less common.
explanation.quickTip: For an outcome claim, prefer the detail that measures the outcome itself rather than a possible reason for it.

questions.hint: Look for the result that directly measures late arrival, not the sentence explaining why some workers may have arrived more easily.

questions.prompt: Match each result to the claim it can support in Park's argument.

items.text: 38% to 17% of inbound trucks waited more than fifteen minutes.
11.8% to 6.4% of morning clock-ins were more than five minutes late.
Orders processed per labor hour changed from 21.4 to 21.1.

zones.label: Productivity was maintained at about the previous level

explanation.answer: Truck waiting → congestion; late clock-ins → punctuality; orders per labor hour → productivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each measure answers a different question. The evidence becomes useful only when it is matched to the exact claim it measures.
explanation.quickTip: Translate the claim into a measurement question: What number would need to change if this claim were true?

questions.prompt: Which detail most directly supports the claim that staggered starts improved employee punctuality?

options.text: The entrance queue averaged fourteen vehicles during the pilot.
options.whyWrong: This supports the congestion claim, not punctuality.

options.text: Some workers said the later shift allowed them to catch a different bus.
options.whyWrong: This may help explain punctuality, but it does not directly measure whether late arrivals became less common.

options.text: Late morning clock-ins fell from 11.8 percent before the pilot to 6.4 percent during it.
Employees were allowed to request which start time they preferred.
options.whyWrong: This is a design limitation, not evidence that punctuality improved.

explanation.whyCorrect: The clock-in comparison directly measures the outcome named in the claim: fewer workers arriving late.
explanation.quickTip: A related explanation is not automatically the strongest evidence. Prefer the measure that directly answers the claim.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports Park's narrower claim that congestion improved without a large productivity loss?

options.text: Truck waits above fifteen minutes fell from 38 percent to 17 percent, while orders per labor hour changed only from 21.4 to 21.1.
Some employees could catch a later bus, and the road construction ended during the third week.
options.whyWrong: These details concern commuting and a possible traffic confound; they do not jointly measure congestion and productivity.

options.text: Late clock-ins fell to 6.4 percent, and damaged-order reports stayed nearly unchanged.
options.whyWrong: This pair addresses punctuality and one productivity-related measure, but not the congestion part of the claim.

options.text: The pilot lasted eight weeks, and workers could request their preferred start time.
options.whyWrong: These details describe the study design rather than evidence for the claimed operational results.

explanation.whyCorrect: The claim contains two parts, so the best evidence must address both: substantially shorter truck waits and nearly unchanged output per labor hour.
explanation.quickTip: For a two-part claim, check that the evidence covers both parts rather than proving only one.

questions.prompt: Which pair contains one piece of evidence for each of Park's two reasons that the pilot deserves a longer trial: lower congestion and better punctuality?

options.text: The entrance queue fell from twenty-six vehicles to fourteen; late clock-ins fell from 11.8 percent to 6.4 percent.
Orders per labor hour changed from 21.4 to 21.1; damaged-order reports stayed nearly unchanged.
options.whyWrong: Both details concern productivity or output quality, not one congestion measure plus one punctuality measure.

options.text: The road construction ended during the pilot; employees could request a preferred start time.
options.whyWrong: These are limitations or confounding factors, not evidence for the two benefits.

options.text: Some workers used a later bus; truck waiting above fifteen minutes fell to 17 percent.
options.whyWrong: The truck-wait figure directly supports congestion, but the bus comment is an explanation for some workers rather than the direct punctuality result.

explanation.whyCorrect: The queue count directly measures congestion and the clock-in rate directly measures punctuality, giving one clear evidence line for each reason.
explanation.quickTip: When the question names two reasons, make sure the pair supplies direct evidence for both—not two facts about the same issue.
